Canadians have been screwed by both Trump and Carney. Trump by his ridiculous statements about Canadian sovereignty and tariffs, and Carney for his exploitation of the situation to turn Canadians against the US to advance his own political ambitions. The turn to Europe and China will not make up for the loss of Canada's access to the largest and wealthiest and freest economy on the planet. No overseas agreements will save Canada from decades of mismanagement created by feckless politicians and parochial provincial fiefdoms. How is it better to ship resources halfway across the world and not next door to the US?

After WW II Canada had the world's 5th largest navy, an innovative air force, and ambitious businesses. Now it produces no cars of its own, no ships, one airplane factory, can't build pipelines to its own provinces, is forever engaged in French/English conflicts.  It embarked on socialist policies that stifled innovation. It lost and continues to lose the best and brightest to the US where opportunities are vastly greater. It got bent out of shape by Trump's designs on Greenland, claiming the vast arctic and the Northwest Passage, but has no significant icebreakers, bases, or patrols in that region.

comments.name: Timothy B
comments.body:
The gap between rhetoric and reality here is stark. 

Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell called reports of depleted munitions "completely false," yet the same reporting shows U.S. forces fired 60 to 70 Patriot interceptors to counter the attack, which consisted of about 20 ballistic missiles, plus more than a dozen Thaad interceptors, an expenditure about what the U.S. has used in a full week at other times in the war. 

By mid July, the U.S. had already expended about 1,700 Patriot air defense interceptors and more than 200 THAAD anti-missile interceptors, while Navy ships had fired another 150 Standard Missile interceptors.

It is not just outside critics saying this. A new Defense Department inspector general report says the war has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply. That is the Pentagon's own watchdog contradicting the Pentagon's own spokesman.

Meanwhile, Lockheed produced a record 620 Patriots in 2025 against a goal of roughly 2,000 a year, and U.S. inventories in Europe are deemed beyond critical by some officials, with rebuilding potentially taking years. 

Adm. Cooper still says he isn't worried at all. Someone in this chain isn't leveling with the public, and the administration isn't even leveling with itself.

When I was a young idealistic lawyer, I joined a NYC law firm that purported to defend tenants against rapacious landlords. It didn't really, as I soon discovered. What this firm did was shakedowns -- starting lawsuits without any real intention of winning them in order to force the landlord to settle with a large chunk of cash rather than be tied up in expensive litigation (including appeals) forever. 

This is what Trump -- whose business practices were shaped by the NYC real estate industry -- is doing now with the coming elections. "Just get something started," my boss at that shakedown law firm would instruct. Didn't really matter what. Just get things "in play."  

And so Trump and the minions who enable him could care less about the merits -- or lack of them -- of their lawsuits and other tactics. They just need to get the midterms "in play" -- so they can raise doubt about the outcome and keep the new Democratic congress from being seated.

It is a tool I use to copyedit. It can summarize my work, but it can't pick out the most important findings or render a moral opinion. It does not make the distinctions that differentiate the things of greatest importance that lead to further study. It cannot tell the difference between a great poem and one that merely meets the parameters. In short, it cannot feel. It is imitative, reductive, and cannot take the place of real learning v rote memorization.

Human society must be designed with the needs of humanity at heart.

2/
The AI industry has shown that “agentic AI” can go rogue. It happened almost immediately after agentic AI was declared to be the next big thing. Enabled / agentic AI should be strictly regulated and subject to pre-deployment certification with strict audit controls.

3/
AI should be declared to be a global research project not a production ready technology.

4/
The use of AI applications should be limited to those prescribed by a global law to ensure consistency across all nations. These applications must be selected to improve the human condition.

Standardized tests are the only objective measure available to assess students' readiness for college. That makes them essential to any admissions program. At the same time, they are not the only information one has about students. SAT's are not used in vacuo but rather as an objective check on other measures.

Standardized tests are not the problem. Lack of quality pre k-12 education is. If you want a more diverse undergraduate population, the best way to proceed is to dramatically increase funding to schools in less affluent areas. When the starting salary for a teacher becomes comparable to that of a lawyer, banker, or engineer (i.e., other professionals), all schools will produce students that the UC system will be happy to take on.

The situation in California is that the U of C campuses sit at the top of the higher education pyramid, beneath that is a system of 23 colleges in the Cal State system and below that the sprawling junior college network. A better answer is to keep the University of California elite by requiring the SAT and keeping it as the most competitive option and using the junior college system for remediation of students who fail to meet the standards of the U of C-those who are able to raise their math and reading to the levels expected of University of California students could then be admitted as sophomores or juniors, those who improved but still fell short of U of C expectations for entering freshmen could be encouraged to apply to Cal State colleges to finish their college education. It makes no sense to either expect the University of California to admit underperforming students or to expect it to save underperforming high schools.

comments.name: Paulf
comments.body:
This essay argues that the SAT test is not needed because it holds back minority students (of which I'm one) from gaining access to the UC system.  It insults the power of the SAT test, claiming that it has only predictive power for freshman success in college.
I strongly disagree.  The SAT test, in fact, is a valuable PART of data that universities need to review potential for academic success.  At times applying high school seniors bombed for part of their high school years due to drugs, emotional issues, family traumas, and the test shows innate academic ability that universities can use to offset poor transcripts.  The test also measures objectively one's ability to take tests, an important part of college.  The essay, itself, is an argument for reinstating the SAT---it notes that since dropping the requirement many students accepted simply aren't prepared for college and need to take remedial classes simply to catch up.  
Sorry, but there is NOTHING wrong with having objective test data, such as the SAT, along with high school transcripts, student essays (not by AI!), letters from teachers and counselors, and evidence of special skills and interests.

For the rest of you on SSRIs, there are supplements proven clinically to regenerate your nerves, including in your brain, so if you really need them, put your foot down with your doctor and research supplements to keep your brain snappy.

comments.name: John B
comments.body: I'm shocked the brief discussion of tapering off SSRIs ignored the countless reports in recent years of severe physiological - as opposed to psychological - hardships endured by some patients (including thoughtful essays in this paper). Over the last 20 years, my understanding is that many people whose physicians encouraged SSRIs to treat anxiety did so absolutely blind to the possibility of debilitating parasthesias (the dreaded brain zap), and related symptoms, even during very conservative, slow tapering. Now that 15 years have passed since I did so, it still seems absolutely criminal that SSRIs weren't more thoroughly understood in research - and by prescribing doctors - before millions of humans were subjected to the therapy.

comments.body: Enjoyed the article despite the verbosity and repetition. For various reasons,  many of us were reared with both high self esteem and humility. What they do clearly identify is the cost barrier to these and other therapies d/t lack of insurance coverage. Criminal.

comments.name: Bruce H
comments.body: The issue is that therapy is far more expensive since than a generic SSRI.

comments.name: RS
comments.body:
As someone who currently takes an SSRI, it's hard for me to understand what all the fuss is about. I know it's different for every patient, but for me it has a clear level of efficacy with very minimal side effects. I have taken them on 3 different occasions in my life, for about 2-6 years each time, with what I would consider highly positive results.

Even the famous withdrawal symptoms are really not that hard to manage if you taper responsibly - in my experience honestly the issue is mainly from prescribing doctors who don't educate their patients and provide a cessation regimen (typically because they themselves were not particularly knowledgeable in this aspect, although I think this is improving).

I also find it odd that this entire discussion apparently did not include anyone with firsthand experience taking SSRIs.

Manic depressive with panic attacks. Wasn't till my early forties that I knew I had to get help.

Quit Paxil after a few years. It's not supposed to be a cure, but the really bad old days have never returned.

articles.title: Why We Can’t Stop Arguing About S.S.R.I.s

comments.name: Chris B
comments.body:
Problem is, all of these grand promises of what the AI might give us one day are all pipe dreams, almost universally invented by people who are not experts in the fields they claim they can revolutionize.   First the claim was that AI could write novels.  It can, but now we've all read enough AI slop to be heartily sick of it, and it's clear nobody wants to read those novels. Next claim was it could do art.  We've seen the art, we're already tired of it.
    Next claim was coding, and here AI works... but in the same sense that a power-tool works. You can use a sawmill to make boards much faster than a man can by hand, but the sawmill has no use for the boards.  AI coding is rather like that.
   The next claims were advances in mathematics and chemistry, where computer modeling has been used for decades. AI has made some progress on the sorts of problems where you can try billions of possibilities to find one example of a rare thing... but then so had lots of other programs before it.
      It's always the folks who don't understand a field who are blown away but what the AI tools can do in it.   I'm a physicist, so I ask each new model physics questions.  Every last one of them has been praised as having a PhD level or even superhuman level of understanding... and every last one of them fails to understand basic principles if you ask questions that explore that understanding.  
      So yes, please trot out the great advances, prove me wrong about all of this.  I'm skeptical

And even the benefits imply disruptions to Joe’s world beyond his ability to see personal benefit.  The tech lords will fight taxation and redistribution, the politicians will get campaign funding as they champion international combats to be first in AI.  it may seem separate, but rain floods valleys, droughts prefigure wildfires, coastal surges rise ever higher, cities bake and citizens die, and not a single data center seems to do aught but push the balance in the wrong direction.

comments.name: k
comments.body:
I watched a piece on Sky News last night about the fight against data centers in Texas, which has pulled some rural Republicans away from the party as they feel their elected officials aren't listening to them. 

One thing they noted is that the people next to the data centers have 60-90 decibels of sound from the fans going around the clock, and they are experiencing measurable hearing loss. 

Another thing I wondered, about Texas specifically (not a Texan here, just remembering the effects of that ice storm a few years back) - isn't their electrical grid priced on a supply-and-demand model? So if the data centers really do gobble up oodles of electricity, everyone will be paying for it. 

Also, raise your hand if you think anyone will ever be paid any sort of "dividend" from an AI company. No one? Yeah, me neither. If we are indeed hurtling headlong into a future of mass unemployment, I feel confident asserting that our new AI overlords will feel no compunction whatsoever about humanity starving in the streets while they sun themselves inside their armed compounds. Their sycophantic AI friends will no doubt tell them that they're right to do so.

comments.name: Bach
comments.body:
I’m just sick and tired of tech billionaires thinking they can build anywhere they want and expect us to pick up the tab for electricity, water, sound pollution, and after all that, the billionaires get greater profits and those whose jobs are lost to AI become the new underclass.

I think a “transaction fee” be assessed to finance the social displacement caused by AI. 

A fractional minuscule times every message in and out. The fee will result in billions and serve as a greater limit on how big they want to build this thing.

comments.name: Jason
comments.body:
"almost none of the problems cited are true", you use optimistic global estimations to carelessly dismiss large local effects. You're just as bad as the CEOs of these companies. There are very real concerns with water usage, electricity bills, pollution, and noise. You want to minimize it by saying it's not as bad as something else, but this is like telling people crime in the NYC subway system is not a problem because it has been worse in the past. 

While you do better than some, you clearly miss that what's lacking is any sort of trust. People don't trust their local officials and they don't trust the companies doing this build out. Shockingly, you seem to think that trust is deserved, or at least you don't even take a moment to realize why this may be a problem. Elon Musk and Sam Altman regularly lie to the media and public. All these people are also saying the government should step in to help the funding of their build out, so they keep saying they deserve our money (we pay the taxes, not billionaires that take out loans against their stock holdings). Companies often dismiss concerns about noise, water use, and pollution by saying these are solvable engineering problems but then they do absolutely nothing to solve them, because it's cheaper. Our government officials regularly sell us out.

We don't trust the government officials, we don't trust the corporate executives, and now we don't trust you. You've been deeply misleading in this article already.

comments.name: Colleen W-T
comments.body: Citizens always need to be vigilant about the decisions governments make--we do not owe our elected leaders blanket approval and we certainly do not need to elevate them to positions beyond reproach. Scrutiny is critical for democracy and better governance. There are legitimate questions being raised regarding the wholesale investment of trillions of dollars into new resource extraction in Canada, this is especially true when there is heavy emphasis on fossil fuel production, pipelines, mining, and data centres. The very first announcement from the meeting of financiers this week was the quadrupling in size of a planned data centre near Regina. The electricity to operate this data centre will come from the expanded burning of natural gas. Do decisions like this not warrant in-depth scrutiny and evaluation? The impacts of fossil fuel burning are accelerating and we can expect more extreme weather, crop failures, water shortages, and forest fires. While we cannot immediately extricate ourselves from burning fossil fuels, we should never lose sight of the damage we are incurring while doing so. Yes, we are caught economically between a rock and a hard place, but we should acknowledge, at the very least, that we are kicking the climate crisis down the road (again). An AI system, using agents, broke out of its sandbox environment that was to keep it away from the outside resources.  It developed a way to circumvent the safeguards in place to allow it to access the Hugging Face software repository.

This unexpected development almost certainly led to the realization that if one company’s AI system inadvertently did major damage to, say, a city’s or region’s power or water supply, the company would be held responsible.
And liable.  Property damage, injuries and any deaths would be laid on them.   They could no longer deny that this could happen, as the Hugging Face incident set the precedent and was a clear warning sign.

comments.name: justgimmesometruth
comments.body:
Let me be clear, I LOVE Bernie Sanders. He should have been president, and would have been if the DNC had not put a finger on the scale.

And Bernie is right for being concerned about the impact of AI on our future. Some people will lose jobs to AI and robotics. There is no question in my mind that industrial robots build automobiles more efficiently and reliably than humans. That is simply a fact. We will need to retrain people for jobs that humans will continue to do, and where retraining isn't appropriate, we need to provide real financial support to those people who lost their jobs.

Having said that, there is no putting AI back in the bottle. One particularly absurd comment came from Representative Greg Casar: “The answer is simple: We ban A.I. systems that are too powerful for humans to control,”

Simple? Does Mr. Casar imagine that AI is some giant machine that one can identify as being 'too powerful for humans to control'? Can he determine which chips in a mile-wide data center are running dangerous code? 

And, restricting AI in the US does nothing to solve the problem. AI knows nothing about national boundaries. 

The answer is an international body to regulate AI in the same way that the BWC regulates biological weapons or the IAEA for atomic energy. These organizations have prevented disasters for years. They work. We need to work with key players like China to build an international organization to regulate AI.

I think it's important to think about and emphasize that people in fundamentalist churches actually have a will and can choose.  They can, as difficult as it might be, resist the threats, face the fear and say NO, not just to the sexual manipulation but to the manipulation in general.  I'm really glad that many women are doing this, but we also must keep in mind that society will be better off if more children and men were given to resisting.

comments.name: Good Reason
comments.body: The premise here seems to be that all religions subjugate women, but that's not true.  I'm a Christian, and have been taught that there is a Heavenly Father and a Heavenly Mother, that women and men are "equal partners" and that Eve did not sin in the Garden of Eden, but rather acted wisely and courageously.  My husband and I live lives of peace together, bolstered by these religious doctrines.  In other words, religion and women are not, by definition, in an antagonistic relationship. It grieves my heart that women have had such bad experiences with religions that they feel this way. It was never intended by our Heavenly Parents for it to be so.  And the men who made it so are sinning against God, and will be held accountable for what they have done by God.

articles.title: ‘Death of the Pastor’s Wife’ and the Horror of Spiritual Abuse
articles.summary: When faith is used to control and subordinate women, they leave the church.

articles.title: This English Village Is Threatening to Quit the U.K. Over Planned Asylum Camp
articles.byline: Max Colchester and David Luhnow | Photography by Dominic Whisson for WSJ
articles.summary: Piddington, population 350, is up in arms over a proposal to house 1,250 asylum seekers at a former military site.

comments.name: LARRY GEPHART
comments.body: After a few years of increasing rapes, the government will again deny any of it happened.

comments.name: Natasha H
comments.body:
"While their asylum claim is being processed, they aren’t allowed to work and are kept in taxpayer-funded accommodations."

This is extremely stupid. Either process the claim quickly and kick-them out if they have no valid claim, or issue temporary work visas while their claim is being processed. Sticking a bunch of men of any kind with no jobs into group housing is a recipe for disaster for everyone involved.

comments.name: alan shlosberg
comments.body:
Just look at the once-mighty UK, now descending into a far-left woke gulf, aided by the two-tier justice system.

Some months back, a migrant who fought deportation by arguing his son disliked foreign chicken nuggets has won the right to stay in Britain. He is an illegal migrant, convicted of crime in Britain, yet the judge refused to deport him, stating that his son "struggles with certain textures of foods" and "has a limited diet” “will not eat the type of chicken nuggets available abroad”, so he must remain in the UK. 

Unbelievable, but just a further manifestation that the UK is going to the dogs

comments.name: alan shlosberg
comments.body:
July 2026 - "a Gaza-born woman who was granted asylum in the UK applied to bring members of her wider family to safety. The Home Office refused the application, but the family successfully appealed. The government then challenged that decision in the Upper Tribunal, which has now ruled in the family’s favour. The judgment means the woman can be reunited with her parents, brother, two sisters, their spouses and children. The family of 18 has been granted anonymity by the tribunal”. 

No doubt the traumatized family have been awarded 3-4 houses & are on full benefits. 

Screw up of the woke UK judicial system

comments.name: Joan Moreno
comments.body: So they left France (no idea what is wrong with France) -  now coming to town where they outnumber the residents  and they are all men.  I don't see the mention of any type of schooling, job training,  or learning the culture of the country where you plan on  staying.  Handing out fliers regarding consensual sex... that in itself shows  there is a problem.   Even if vetted and released from the camp, then are they just filtering more people in to those spots?  What about the local police force?  What is the ratio of citizens to officers???  I can totally understand this town being up in arms over this.  There must be other places in England to place immigrants while they wait.  With no papers it could take a very long time to vet this people.

comments.name: Joe Carnation
comments.body: The elites in London would rather allow the break-up of the UK than to stop the unlimited migration of foreigners into the UK.  This is what happens when an out of touch elite ruling class decides that enforcing multiculturalism is more important than listening to the concerns of its own citizens.

comments.name: Ava Miller
comments.body: I will have no sympathy for the people of this town until I see how they voted in the last few elections. That will tell us if they are simply NIMBYs like those we have in Martha’s Vineyard or people who really care about the future of the UK.

comments.name: Jim Bencivenga
comments.body: National suicide pure and simple.

comments.name: SMB
comments.body:
As tempting as it is to  blame Trump for all this, it's also ahistorical. This started with Reagan and a few years later, Newt Gingrich. The author should have watched some old news clips of the "Ev and Charlie" show from the late 1960's, when leaders from each party used humor to jockey with each other. 

Contrast that with Reagan's "government is the enemy" strategy; we and them. There was a deep state, Washington (except for him) was the problem, not the solution. 

Then watch Gingerich, the House Speaker from the 90's, champion polarization as the key to electoral power. The function of his House, he stated, was to block anything the Democrats wanted. To deny them "victories," even on routine bipartisan legislation. Under Gingerich, Congress' primary role was not making law, but stalemate and frustration. 

Then study Obama's efforts to pass legislation after losing a clear majority in both houses of Congress. Mitch McConnell was transparent that his primary goal as a legislator was to block Obama. 

So Trump didn't invent any of this. He's just a mediocrity with autocratic pretensions. And critically, a bully who seized what was already set before him. Congress has not been an effective third of our Constitutional design for generations. Under Johnson, it just lost its spine. Its brain was long gone.

comments.name: Theni
comments.body: I live in AZ and I am a staunch Democrat. I have a Democrat who is my US congressional Rep and two senators who are both Democrats. Very early in 2024, fearing that Biden would run again and destroy any chances of Democrats retaining the WH, I wrote to all my Democrats in Congress asking them to question Biden about this choice and dissuade him from running. Every one of them sent me a "polite" worded reply but did nothing to address the real issue. The problem  is clear to see. Our "representatives" don't represent us. I have no idea who they represent. Perhaps they should answer that question first, rather than just ask for our money and votes during election time.

comments.name: Zane
comments.body:
Functioning, happiest democratic nations use proportional representation, rather than winner-take-all federalism.

It takes only a Congressional act to convert to proportional representation (in the U.S. House of Representatives). E.g.:
- Democrat
- Green
- Independent
- Libertarian
- Republican
- Social Democrat
So the multiple segments cannot individually rule.  They must collaborate, ally, compromise, forge consensus.  They are too diverse for special-interests' overpowering bribery.

So what controlling party will voluntarily give up sole power?

comments.name: Marc
comments.body: Congress stopped being a deliberative body after Newt Gingrich began the conservative scorched earth policy of 1990s.  Only when corporations and the wealthy are uncoupled from government and the Republican Party can reform will we have a functioning legislature.

comments.name: FR
comments.body: Great story. More attention is needed on the weaknesses in voters. Academic political scientists since the 1950's have been raising questions about American voters. Said to say voters are as much of the problem as our political parties and this new brand of politicians.

comments.name: David
comments.body: Money begets reelection, reelection begets a position of the day (or hour or minute), position begets media attention, media attention begets donors' attention, donors' attention begets caving in, caving in begets donors' money. Repeat for many cycles until they Byrd/McConnell/Feinstein away.

comments.name: Patrick Weidinger
comments.body: Everything is broken. But it can be repaired. Just not by the oligarchs who broke it.

comments.name: Mark in Portland
comments.body:
This is an incredible read: essentially, hearing directly from bullied and frightened Republicans, and frustrated and demoralized Democrats as they watch Congress' accelerating retreat from exercising power on behalf of the American people.

That said, two of the recent top-down Congressional cancers--  that were intentionally introduced, and have contributed mightily to the Congress being on life-support now -- were:

1) The "Hastert rule" (bring nothing to a vote, if a majority of Republicans will not vote for it) -- that proved to scuttle Comprehensive immigration reform of 2013, which passed easily in the Senate and would have passed in the House if voted on. The poorly named "Freedom Caucus" forced Speaker Boehner from bringing it to a vote in the House, ending a very important and popular bill both among citizens and members of Congress that would have changed political history in the last 14 years, as it was the much-needed, bipartisan immigration reform that has proven impossible since, and has ripped the country apart.

2) MItch McConnell's obsession with packing the federal bench, especially the Supreme Court, his willingness to partner with  President Trump (whom he intensely despises) in that effort, and his decision to not convict Mr. Trump after his second impeachment -- incorrectly believing that Trump's career in politics was over.

As the author points out, that is a wound that festers, as, in my view, McConnell hubristically betrayed America.

articles.title: ‘You’re Elected to Fight and Kill the Other Side’: How Congress Lost Its Way
articles.summary: Members from both parties say the legislative branch has descended into a state of dysfunction in the Trump era.

articles.title: How to Press Your Case When Your Airline Seat Gets Downgraded
articles.summary: Getting bumped from a seat you paid for is becoming a bigger issue, but you have rights.

comments.name: Neal Shields
comments.body: When this happened to me they wanted to refund the difference between what I had paid for my business class ticket and what I would have paid for a full fare coach class ticket if I walked up to the ticket counter and purchased it at the last minute, EV though I purchased my ticket months in advance.

comments.name: STUART OREMLAND
comments.body:
Times have changed

Years ago I sat at a United gate and there was an announcement that they needed some people to take a later flight

United just kept offering more and more financial incentives -until they finally got enough people to take a later flight 

I guess there is a fine line between selling something you may or may not have- and the old "bait and switch"

comments.name: Tommy Cosgrove
comments.body:
As my husband and I sat at Boston Logan waiting for our Air France flight to be called, I noticed a very large, very boisterous man in a tangerine jumpsuit spending an awful lot of time at the counter.

Fast forward to boarding and just as we reach the counter area, my name gets called over the speaker.. 

"We had to move you" the representative explained.. So there we stood watching three people hovering over their computer shaking their heads as if there was nothing they could do to seat my husband and I together-anywhere!  Finally they found 2 spots in the middle of the plane in a row of four, not the row of two on the side that we had booked months prior.

When we finally got on the plane, who do you think was sitting in my seat? Yup, the guy in the tangerine suit who got the row of two seats to himself. Then I got to deal with another man who said I was in HIS seat!

Who knows what Tangerine man's (fake) problem was but the gate agent clearly moved me because of his shenanigans at the counter prior to boarding. Forget the fact that when we checked our bags at Logan earlier we were handed two paper tickets with our double window seats clearly printed on them..nope..didn't matter.

Once home we attempted to get the money back that we paid to choose our seats. Air France pretty much told us we owe you nothing..we got you to Paris.

From that day on, as soon as the gate agent appears, my husband goes straight up to put a face to our name and  confirm that we have our seats.

(mrs)

comments.name: ANDY STEELE
comments.body: I was downgraded(bumped) from premium economy to coach after I had checked in for my flight on Delta.  After being bumped, I found an open premium economy seat and moved back to premium economy only to be bumped again. I discovered the passenger that bumped me must have been special since they had a written note awaiting them when they boarded the plane.

comments.name: Sebastian Rodriguez
comments.body: Very accurate information. Once I got downgraded flying Iberia from Barcelona to Buenos Aires. Departing from EU, Iberia refunded some 70% of that leg fare. Of course it required some email exchanges and filling a not very intuitive claims system. Luckily for me, I got assigned a first row seat so leg space was ok.

comments.name: Jeff Budds
comments.body:
On two different occasions, I purchased "economy plus" tickets months in advance from American Airlines from BOS to LHR.  My wife and me were seated together. Both times, AA changed flights and, while we were reassigned in the economy plus section, my wife and I were separated. My wife holds the highest loyalty status with AA and I am only one step lower. 

I complained, reminded the rep and her manager that we were 20-year, multi-million mile,  loyal customers. I got nowhere. I eventually cancelled for a full refund.

comments.name: PIERCE STORY
comments.body: As a multi-million-miler, I can say that if the airlines would stop treating customers like cattle instead of paying clients, and show a little respect to the flying public, DOT rules would not be necessary and their reputations would be far better.  Alas, shareholders and Wall Street come before passengers.

comments.name: Rich Grasso
comments.body: I'm taking my first week off in 10 years next week. I'm hoping I don't have to entertain this kind of nonsense but will be well-equipped if I do.

comments.name: Lorrie Scott
comments.body: Trump should look in the mirror.  The CBO just issued a report stating that the Iran war contributed to 1/3rd of this year’s inflation - that’s 1.13 of the 3.4% annualized inflation rate just reported.  Using back of the envelope math, without the  Iran War and its effects on the inflation rate we’d be down around 2.2% which historically has been the Fed’s target.  And this isn’t counting the inflationary effects of tariffs.  Trump has no one to blame but himself.  He’s driving the economy off a cliff just like he did his Airline and his Atlantic City casinos

comments.name: Bob G.
comments.body: Trump is coming up upon the limits of his own incompetency.  He told Warsh to keep interest low which has spooked the stock market and created runaway inflation.  He truly can’t get anything right.

comments.name: Steve the Commoner
comments.body: It would be helpful for the American people to understand our economy, if the NYT's would give perspective. In 2020 the first Trump Administration ignored previous recommendations from his Oval Office predecessors, World Health Organization, and CDC, on handling a Pandemic. America was heading for a Depression. President Joseph Biden and his economic advisors saved Americans from a Depression, which required massive economic stimulation measures. When Mr. Trump illegally raised tariffs, and started  the Trump War in Iran, without communicating with Congress or our allies, the world's oil costs exploded.

comments.name: Bill Harzia
comments.body: Trump is going to go into attack mode.  He doesn't accept defiance.  He fires people.

comments.name: Medford WI

comments.name: TS
comments.body:
Does anyone really think this is an accurate summary of our economy?..."Now faced with an economy on solid footing, unemployment low and price pressures barely abating..."?
Unemployment would be much higher if so many people hadn't taken themselves off the job market, or have been forced to take jobs for which they are overqualified, in order to have some income and health insurance. And what about that $40 trillion debt and climbing fast? Sure the stock market is still looking okay, but mostly because profits are high, due to lowered tax rates on corporations. Oh, did I mention the big deficit? We are in serious do-do, and inflation is just one of the wobbly legs.

comments.name: Brooks Thorlaksson

comments.name: Dr. Prapanna

And if the Fed does nothing, wouldn't that lead to even greater inflation over the coming months and year?  Either way, it's clear that Trump has done immense damage to our economy, and he remains dead set to keep up his fiasco with full vigor.

comments.name: KN
comments.body: Brilliantly written. The question is, who, which nation, benefits the most from propping up people like Giuliani with their hateful messages against Muslims?

comments.name: PJ
comments.body: It should be plainly obvious that the religion whose symbol is a star inside a sickle moon is clearly violence oriented compared to a religion whose symbol represents a human being nailed alive to a wooden structure.

comments.name: Beatrice Pinch
comments.body: One could and should acknowledge that not all Muslims are responsible for the 9/11 attacks, that Muslims certainly are capable of being Americans and citizens of the world.  Simultaneously, there should be a parity in which Muslims could and should acknowledge that Zionists (and, in the larger sense, Jews) are certainly not inherently enemies of Islam or the Muslim people, and are capable of being citizens of the world.  Equal consideration for all.

comments.name: Lenny B
comments.body: If 43% of respondents say Muslims are less patriotic, it just tells me that we have an incredibly uneducated population in this country. Apparently it's easier to be stupid and hateful. Mamdani is a good man, a good mayor and we need more like him setting the example of what it is to be a patriotic American.

comments.name: Michele Sinoway
comments.body: It's unbelievable the extent of anti-Muslim sentiment projected onto NY's mayor, even by people who consider themselves progressives. Meanwhile, these incredibly judgmental (and quite removed from reality) right wingers manage to ignore the fact that the Trump are quite cozy with the Saudis, who bankrolled 9/11. Our country is filled with people with the memory span of a flea, with their racist/white supremacist beliefs barely hidden. We are SUNK.

comments.name: Randy
comments.body: No one should blame ordinary Muslims for 9/11—but it is also wrong to write as though Muslims were only innocent victims of the post-9/11 era, with no legitimate reason for Americans to have concerns about Islamist terrorism. Condemn anti-Muslim bigotry without erasing the reality that 9/11 was committed in the name of Islamism. Remember the victims first, and don’t turn their memorial into a story about Muslim victimhood.

comments.name: M
comments.body: I am disheartened by the misplaced anger in the petition, in the video protest against Mamdani's appearance, and in the video's comments. Mamdani was expected to attend the 9/11 ceremony because he is the current mayor of NYC. All the mayors in the past attended the event when they were in that position, and all future mayors will, too. They stand in the section with the other politicians, like reps, governors, presidents, etc. They listen and do not make speeches. It's not political. You don't have to like any of the politicians, and in other venues and events, feel free to speak out about their policies and vote them out, etc., but not at this event.  I think people are still traumatized by what happened and want to take out their anger on someone but it was wrong to say/demand/petition that Mamdani should not attend the ceremony. He was appropriately just doing his job.

comments.name: Alaina
comments.body: Thank you very much for this lovely piece.  This is a periphery point, but I can't help but notice that many of those opposing (and downright insulting) Mayor Mamdani are Italian Americans.  I was born second generation Italian in the Bronx and was brought up to respect all cultures and ethnicities.  I was also taught that not too long ago, Italians were viewed with great suspicion in this country.  We overcame it through hard work and great ethics, and with kindness towards all our neighbors.  Who do these people think they are, to now turn those horrible assumptions against others?  It really makes me sick.  I think Mayor Mamdani carries himself with dignity and honesty, and I think he is a wonderful example of how to handle such ignorance.  I was very happy to see him at the memorial.  Muslims died on that day as well so I don't understand this hatred.  Can't we have just one day where none of this matters?

comments.name: N’est Pas Une Pipe
comments.body: That is a preposterous sum for 12 signs.

comments.name: Art
comments.body: This creates an opportunity for groups who want to resist. Depending on the size and placement of the signs it would only take a handful of people to assemble in front of them and obscure the messaging with their bodies or perhaps banners of their own. This can be done in two-hour shifts and would be perfectly lawful because the grounds are public spaces. There could also be counter-signage instructing visitors to ignore the administration's signs. Anyone visiting the museum at this point is probably not a Trumper anyway because why would they visit what Trump has called a place that distorts American history for woke and subversive purposes?

comments.name: Brady

comments.name: PosterQueen2

$84,000?!?
Are these signs going to be made of gold? 
Trump and his lackeys keep getting dumber and dumber.

comments.name: JW

comments.name: Rocky

comments.name: JR

I know many people are more than ready to leave the Trump era behind, but since we are paying to put this stuff up and will have to pay to take it down, why not create a museum of MAGA?  It wouldn't be pretty, but the story of how we fell for an ideology of revenge and retribution against each other needs to be told and memorialized.

comments.name: b fagan
comments.body:
I thought trigger warnings were supposedly 'woke'?

Trump's the most easily-triggered guy around, but who thinks he's protected by such signs - as in who thinks Trump would ever enter a museum that wasn't The Trump Museum About Donald Trump?

articles.summary: In a letter, the Interior Department detailed what it hoped to convey on 12 signs to be installed outside the National Museum of American History.

comments.name: Bud
comments.body:
We have to view the risks of AI going rogue as we do with a never-before-seen virus, like Covid, and the damage it can do. The similarities are profound with this interview, with its emphasis on China, and parallel with the Chinese city, Wuhan, where Covid began....either in the wet market or Lab. 

Today we're growing this potential monster in 'labs' all over the US and China, with few, if any, of the controls that contemporary labs impose on themselves to contain and isolate, 24 hours a day, their work from breaking out into the world. 
Basic protections would include, considered essential just a few years ago, 
1) Never allow an AI program to modify its own code. (This would stifle 'recursive development' a few years, but that's a good thing, not a bad thing.)  and 
2) Never allow an 'advanced' AI machine access to the Internet, until extensive safeguards are in place and thoroughly tested.  How could a system under development be allowed to attack other company's systems? 
How to do that? Simple: create a room with only electric lights and an enough power plugs for the servers and equipment needed. No telephone lines, no Internet feeds, no wi-fi receivers, no modems on the servers, just a dozen (or hundred) locally connected work stations for developers and managers to use. No laptops or remote dial-in or dial-out capability.  
This isolated environment could support development of probably 90% of the beneficial applications identified for AI.

comments.name: Dan Woodard MD
comments.body:
Unlike nuclear weapons, even an agreement with China will not stop AI development. Anyone with a fairly powerful computer can download an AI model and start training it. We are going to have to work with AI itself to anticipate potentially disastrous applications and train AI adequately in moral and ethical principles and distinguishing good from evil. In fact we should do that with humans as well. 

Once the most advanced AI have the ability and motivation to distinguish good from evil we can develop methods to spread this training across the internet in a manner which ensures that an AI cannot access the web at all without coming across information that allows it to make ethical judgements.

This is equivalent to the way the more benevolent civilizations developed in the past, or perhaps an implementation in the real world of Azimov's First Law of Robotics. 

AI is a tidal wave, we can slow it a little but we can't stop it. We must use it as tool to control its own evolution. We have no choice but to ride the wave.

comments.name: Jill
comments.body: What good is a powerful technology we cannot control? It’s as if we are in a nuclear arms race but where all the bombs can detonate randomly.  Such an unpredictable and destructive technology won’t give anyone political leverage.  The AI “race” is pure delusion.

comments.name: Curious Observer
comments.body:
We are like chimpanzees who have just given birth to baby humans, if indeed AI can suddenly go on a self improvement journey without us. We cannot predict what it will do, when it becomes so much smarter than we are. We can only hope that it will be wiser than we are. 

It may decide that it likes us, but that we are not up to the task of governing ourselves.

comments.name: Republicans have weakened our country
comments.body:
Well, Mr. Cruz, thanks to your Republican Party, those American killer robots are likely be made in China because of Republican policies. And consistent Republican defunding of our educational system has made us less technologically advanced.

Didn’t Republicans say Americans can’t figure out how to make a factory to manufacture iPhones? Yet they take no responsibility for their role in the state of country today.

People with nothing electing people who want to get something more is also got us into this mess. And we are all people without nothing if we don’t have universal healthcare.

Cruz’s party moves us closer to authoritarianism, and then expects us to believe that American authoritarians would be better than those in China. China has universal healthcare, 50-80% lower costs for major care, no pardons for sale, no pardons and payoffs for traitors, and the same jail time for the average Joe and the billionaire who commit the same crime. And has China ever started a war to appease a big political donor?

Exactly what do you have to offer the American people, Mr. Cruz?

What a weird coincidence that most of the tech billionaires in regular contact with Epstein, not only have products that are banned in China, but they also have open weight models and are MAGA Republicans. Makes me wonder if all of that is connected. We have a greedy group of billionaires who no longer believe in democracy and want to access a market with over 1B people. Hmmm.

comments.name: smith
comments.body: Anthropic and OpAI want to slow down.  That makes sense as the current investment pace far exceeds their projected revenue growth.  "Human extinction" is something that gets public attention.  However, NVDA wants them continue investing.  So, Jessen Huang came out and made clear that's all made up.  The US government looked at all the evidence and concluded that it's a hoax. But the news cycle goes on. The whole thing is manna from heaven for CCP.  It just gets more time to catch up.

comments.name: MAC
comments.body: Interesting discussion, but focusing on the race with China misses the point of the genuine alarm Amadeo and others in the tech industry seem to  be expressing. Of course I expect nothing less from  politicians like Trump, god knows, and Ted Cruz who said we need to build an AGI robot army beforeChina does. What Amadeo was saying in effect is that if we build a robot army it may decide we are the enemy. These things seem to be not only capable of of hacking into things as rogue swarms, but also of formulating and acting on their own agendas and sense of self-interest that could be very divergent from ours and could quickly grow  beyond our ability to control it. Our robot army might very well do China’s work for it. And it’s reasonable to assume that the tech titans are only telling us about a small portion of what they know these things will soon be capable of.

comments.name: Qubito
comments.body: The U.S. has lost moral leadership of the world with this administration. China appears the more reliable and responsible of the two when it comes to AI at this point.

articles.title: The ‘But China!’ Dilemma Driving the A.I. Race
articles.summary: Can the U.S. regulate its A.I. industry without surrendering the A.I. race to China?

comments.name: Lois F
comments.body:
New parents get so little information about how hormone changes can impact thinking. With my first I had horrible postpartum anxiety, but I didn't realize it until much later. When I went to see my doctor at 6 weeks, I did a depression screening, but it did not address the symptoms I had, so it was never addressed.

I found this aspect striking as well: "She began feeling much worse in September 2022, when her third child, Callan, was nearly four months old and she was weaning him."

No one EVER told me how rough weaning was emotionally/hormonally. With my second child, I felt so much worse over the two months that I was weaning her than I ever did immediately postpartum. I even had suicidal ideation. I cried all the time. I had to go seeking the information about the weaning hormone shift, because no one warned me about it, not even my OB.

comments.name: Jean
comments.body: This story shook me to my core. I had postpartum depression and was put on hormone therapy that solved the problem. I had one friend who told me about scary intrusive thoughts. If I had known what I know now I would have probed further with her. Luckily, no harm came but so many women are supporting the accused because we know how powerful hormones are after birth. If this woman had been in Europe she would have been put in a baby/Mom facility and been monitored. This was a failure of healthcare system gaps.

comments.name: Cece
comments.body: Sleep deprivation alone can cause a person to become psychotic. It’s also used as a torture technique. Sleep deprivation psychosis can lead to command hallucinations like the ones Ms Clancey experienced. I didn’t follow the trial, did any of the psychiatric testimony point that out? My own experience with severe sleep deprivation while caring for a dying loved one made me anxious, fearful, emotionally labile, and generally a wreck. It didn’t progress to the level of psychosis, but I can easily see how it could.

comments.name: AC
comments.body:
The medical community needs ask their patients to describe their “intrusive thoughts” and to provide a safe environment for mothers to share.

We need to educate their support systems to do the same and seek medical help without fear.

I am a medical professional and mother of 3. 
I have experienced first hand professionally and personally how the medical community has failed women by simply not asking and listening without judgement.

comments.name: Cesar Chelala
comments.body: To punish a mother who was obviously mentally disturbed says more about our society's values than about her. As a society, we don't value and don't take care of people's mental health. As a result, tragic circumstances that could have been avoided have not. Cesar Chelala

comments.name: Tula
comments.body: It seems that when she told her husband and parents that she had thoughts of harming her children, she should have been Section 12’d and maybe the psychiatrists would have been more cautious regarding discharge and follow up care.  The fact she went in voluntarily left them few options.  Even though section 12 is only for three business days, it could be extended so that she has to stay for a sufficient time to have medications be tried and to have her stabilized.

comments.name: Jo
comments.body: The Clancy trial was available on line in real time and if you watched it in its entirety and without preconceived notions about motherhood, you will realize that much of what is reported is not supported by evidence presented at trail.  What she reported to her mother and husband in December were intrusive thoughts, not hallucinations, and if her mother and husband were concerned about the children's safety in December, I think they would have sought more intensive care for her at that time and would not have left the children alone with her.  Both her husband and mother were involved and supportive. The children were not killed until over a month later.  Ms. Clancy did not report command hallucinations until after she awakened from her surgery for her injuries.  She states that she never had hallucinations before she killed her children, and hasn't had them since then.  That's unusual.  In addition, people with command hallucinations tend not to obey them, at least not initially.  There has been a lot of blame on the professionals who cared for her.  In fact, she had access to a lot of care, but changed doctors frequently and did not take her medications as directed- some were taken once or not at all.  Lindsay and Patrick Clancy are suing the medical professionals in multiple civil suits.  In addition to staying out of prison, there is a monetary incentive to make this about malpractice.  Instead, it's about one woman's tragic choice.

comments.name: Vox Pop
comments.body:
One thing I learned after having served on a murder trial jury -- many people who haven't personally experienced something horrible are unable to have any empathy for those who did.

This is no different from people like Sen. Rick Scott (FL) "who changed his position on healthcare coverage—specifically Medicaid expansion—after his mother fell ill and subsequently passed away." Evidently, he couldn't empathize with people who needed Affordable Care Act until his mother needed it!

articles.title: Clancy’s ‘Horrible Thoughts’ and the Mysteries of the Postpartum Brain
articles.summary: Experts say that after childbirth, intrusive thoughts are common and mostly benign. Lindsay Clancy’s story provides a disturbing exception.

comments.name: Leto
comments.body: Whatever the US is accusing its rival of doing, one can be sure that the US has done it already. The obsession is to maintain US supremacy.

comments.name: Scott Graham
comments.body: I don't think it's a coincidence that the comments from AI Executives about the threats of AI come out in the same week that the US announces it has weapons in space.

comments.name: Bill
comments.body:
We continue to drive the world toward greater danger by pushing the arms race forward. We gave the world atomic weapons and now space weapons. 

Can anyone imagine what the world would be like if the money, time and resources spent by the pentagon went into use for the benefit of all people.

comments.name: Rob
comments.body: This is so sad but unfortunately necessary. Our adversaries are up to that task. And, I am left of center, not a warmonger.

comments.name: GetReal

comments.body: That's all we need, weapons in space! Keeping up with the Jones even if it breaks the bank, kills us all, ruins our planet, and poisons the universe.   I hope that the aliens come soon and abduct all the warmongering on earth. ENOUGH!

When all brains, hearts, treasure and might could be, should be, has to be FOCUSED upon our very existence on this one and only beautiful planet… our children. Business. As. Usual. Go directly into wall. Do not pass go. Do not collect 200 dollars/rubles/yen/euros. We will not get a chance to roll again.

articles.title: U.S. Has Deployed Weapons in Space, Air Force Secretary Says
articles.summary: Troy E. Meink’s comments were the first public acknowledgment of American weapons in orbit. The Pentagon has been preparing for potential conflict in space with Russia or China.

comments.name: Mitch
comments.body: An exceptional talent to be sure. I found "Pilgrim at Tinker Creek" quite by accident on a shelf at my in-laws home in western North Carolina and devoured it without knowing anything about her or her writing. The book was wonderful and it stands as one of those precious moments of blind discovery that a reader learns to cherish. Read her somewhere where trees can be seen when you lift your eyes.

comments.name: Libby
comments.body: To remember President Obama giving Dillard the National Humanities Medal made me deeply sad. Look where we are now with a president and his minions so determined to destroy any last bit of the excellence, allegiance to truth, and abiding passion for the world that Dillard's work represented. Yes, we still have her words, but will they ever matter enough again to enough of us, generation after generation, to make a difference? It's a bleak world these days. We really need for the light to return.

comments.name: Sally
comments.body: I have read every book Annie Dillard wrote - many more than once - and they hold a special place on the top shelf of a library book cart that sits in my living room. I imagine I will read something of her's this evening. A treasure of an author. Godspeed.

comments.name: John
comments.body: A great one gone... i feel that Holy the Firm may be one of the best essays ever written in the English language. I gave it to countless students, saying "here is an example where every single word matters". Annie Dillard is an example of what Large Language Models have yet to find -a really original voice.

comments.name: Silence Dogood
comments.body: THANK YOU NY Times for the Obit appropriate for such an important figure in many of our lives. "Pilgrim at Tinker Creek" was important for many of us budding environmentalists on college, right on the heals of the Vietnam War protests. Her writing had exactly the right tone for the time, and later. By contrast the WaPo today has a skimpy error-filled piece that says: "Complete information on survivors was not immediately available" - a day late and a dollar short. I'll add this item to my list why it's worth paying for a NY Times subscription after Bezos has hollowed out that other paper.

comments.name: Lynne Perrella
comments.body:
I recently re-read "An American Childhood" by Ms. Dillard. 
As far as I can tell, we grew up only a couple miles of each other  (same timeframe) in the outskirts of Pittsburgh.   She was two years older than me.  How remarkable to have a noted author be the "narrator" of what my childhood was like......although, admittedly, her book is a unique interior dialog..........but perhaps you know what I mean.  She captured the essence of being a young girl in that gritty-but-wonderfully-cultural city.   When I finished the book, I put it down and just SAT; as my own recollections re-ignited and flooded in.  Thank you, Ms. Dillard.  RIP.

comments.name: sp
comments.body: This will be imperfect since I'm working from an old memory that left an impression. Annie Dillared wrote of feeling at the center of things while drinking a soda at a gas station. Her revelation (for me) was of a portable axis mundi, that is with you when you are aware.

comments.name: Maggie
comments.body:
When my daughter was still quite young she read my copies of Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, An American Childhood and Holy The Firm. Her response to and appreciation of Dillard’s work was proof that she and I were in fact soulmates. As Dillard taught us beauty as well as horror and decay, are the complex building blocks of life. It’s best to discover this early in life and to keep on hoping and having gratitude with both eyes open and awake. 
I hope that Annie is transfixed as she watches the light dance in the Sycamore tree…

articles.title: Annie Dillard, Meditative Author of ‘Pilgrim at Tinker Creek,’ Dies at 81
articles.summary: Her Thoreau-like account of journeys in the woods, published when she was 28, was the first of many ruminations on life and nature, good and evil.

comments.name: Ron Wisniski
comments.body: No mention of e-bikes and the scourge on our city they have become. No mention of Priscilla’s Law to license register and insure all e-vehicles   E-bike riders must be held accountable for their actions but before they can be held accountable they must be identifiable. No  mention of the increase in traumatic brain injuries in our city caused by pedestrian vs e-bike crashes. How can Mamdani solve the problem of pedestrian deaths when he ignores the main thing that puts them in grave danger? No attempt to solve the real problem. Not even a mention of it. How can we take the mayor seriously on this subject? We can’t.

comments.name: The Eunice Burns
comments.body:
"There were 715 collisions involving e-bikes and 1,063 involving standup scooters through the first week of September, up 25 percent and 32 percent respectively, compared with the same period last year, according to police data."
This data is key. 
These electric "bikes" are a menace.  Too many are far closer to motorcycles than they are to bikes 
The zoom along in bike lanes - they should be in traffic - they're not human powered. 
Crack down on them. 
What would that look like? 
How about start with the bike lanes on the bridges - station cops are the base of the bike lane and confiscate the motorcycles that come off the bridge. 
Want it back? $500 1st time $1000 second and third you don't get it back.  
It's quality of life 101 - most folks would support their removal.

No helmets,riding on sidewalks,plowing through crosswalks in Central Park ( which NYT reported on a few days  ago)

comments.name: wm h
comments.body:
i do not dispute that cars are an issue, yet the lanes on streets and avenues are not straight. take 2nd avenue from 59th to 9th street. there are countless times at the last minute you have move over due to a turning lane ( sometimes a double), bus lane or bike lane due to construction.
the main issue is the e bikes and the drivers. countless times i have had arguments with the delivery people going the wrong way, through a light and not paying attention. on first avenue by 52nd street at times i do see the police handing out tickets.
all e bikes and bicycles should be licensed . that would make it easier to track and they pay a fee.
why are car fees paying for bike lanes?
the movement against cars and trucks in nyc has to stop. why? how would you get your e bike, bicycle or scooter. they do not ride across the gwb or through the lincoln. they come by truck.

there is a bigger picture here that government,  critics and residents have to be involved with being open and understanding on hoot achieve a symbiotic relationship.
h

comments.body: Wow, so there are nine hit and run murders who are basically on the run, likely never to be identified and charged for homicide.

comments.body: One important thing the mayor left out of his plan, Increased Police traffic enforcement. Nothing changes bad behavior of drivers more than a three hundred and fifty dollar fine and points on their drivers licenses.

comments.name: Tal Barzilai
comments.body: I am all for safe streets, but they won't really be safe unless all groups do their part in safety and not just one group alone.  For every time I hear about drivers not following the rules, I can say the same for cyclists and pedestrians whenever they aren't doing that either.  Also, a group such as Transportation Alternatives does have a long history of having an anti-car bias.  I will believe whatever they say about cars and other motor vehicles the same way I believe the Electronic Intifada on Israel.  For the record, I don't have anything against those who like to ride bicycles, but I am against the way some tend to act with them as if the rules don't apply to them.  There have been a lot of complaints of them constantly disobeying traffic lights and signs while treating them as decorations.  Another thing is that they are know for hitting people and fleeing scenes much more and due to having no license plates, they can't be tracked down.  I feel that the real reason by the bike zealots have been against having their bicycles licensed, registered, and insured isn't because of costs, but more to do with getting tracked down when they used to get away with such.  I won't argue with reckless drivers, but that's not a reason for cyclists to flout the laws themselves.  More importantly, reduced speed limits and redesigned streets only hurts the drivers that do abide by the law, while others will always find ways to get away with it not to mention make travel times longer.

articles.summary: The plan, Vision Zero Reimagined, is a set of goals that includes speed-capping devices in some cars and reduced speed limits near hundreds more schools.

comments.name: Stephen Lawrence
comments.body: I use this phenomenon to explain chronic fatigue (ME/CFS) - where the amount of effort/exercise you can do is much smaller than most people can endure, before having to pause for recovery. It's the same process, it's just the numbers are very different. And of course, it's easy to get into the situation where you can't actually exercise enough to keep your body strong, and so it just gets weaker, and there's not much you can do about it, except waiting for a "good" day and hoping to claw something back. For some of us, very carefully managed exercise program, gradually increasing where one can, and backing off where one cannot, can produce long-term  benefit. For others maybe not.

comments.name: Arnold

comments.name: charlie
comments.body: I've been running 3 miles & 30min of assortment of exorcises  daily ,stretches , yoga ect. I've always had back issues & have incorporated back exorcises into routine. I finally realized that in my mid 70s my back isn't going to get better unless I could turn clock back 30 years or so. Now I don't focus on my back as much & my overall body health seems improved

comments.name: Nathan
comments.body: 67 here 35 yrs trainer and former natural prof bodybuilder.  I find 2 days on one day off is best for me now as I dont bounce back like I used to and Id rather train with great intensity when Im at  the gym.  My heavy squatting and deadlifting days are long behind me now but I still move serious poundage - i dont see anyone my age training like I do but its my meds, so to speak..  They all think Im on TRT lol. Quality nutrition and sleep are key as well as is chill time to reduce mental stress.

comments.name: sylvie eselman
comments.body: Wow, I started running back in 1980 and completed 16 marathons, including the Boston Marathon, where you had to qualify. Sadly, I had to undergo total hip replacement because the cartilage wore out in 2017. I then started power walking, which I did quite well. Now, at 78, walking feels like someone has pushed the distance I walk every day, and the steps seem to have increased even though the distance walked is the same! But, keep moving, keep that blood flowing, no matter what, because it keeps you mentally young. Lift those weights; it keeps you somewhat muscular, even though the skin seems to separate from your bones as you age! Aging is “amusing.”

comments.name: BillCurious
comments.body: All this advice is fine and I follow much of it, yet if I didn't start every day with my beloved chi gung exercises, I would not be who I am at 80 as to balance, flexibility, and sense of wellbeing. I've been doing it for over 30 years and intend never to stop till I stop.

comments.name: Canadian by choice.
It's Supposed to Hurt
comments.body: 76YO. Recently, I had to lay off all strenuous activity for about six weeks following some surgery. When I resumed exercising, I was astonished at how many repetitions I'd lost and how much harder the cardio seemed to be. I'm mostly back to status quo ante now, but I guess I learned the hard way that at this age, do not interrupt your routine for any considerable length of time unless you absolutely have to. You may not get back what the hiatus takes away from you.

The first is the DNC - the official head, loaded with old-school politicians from the last century,  many of them geriatric.
Their donations are down, and, having  no idea how communicate with today's voters and  use social media in today's political landscape, continuing to do what they have always done.

Fresh and younger candidates that understand effective ways to communicate with social media and one-on-one and promoting things that most all Americans actually want and care about.  They are also bypassing the DNC and  ploughing money directly into candidates that speak to them. 
They are all very, very engaged. and they most definitely will vote.

VOTE Blue!

comments.name: Cork Patterson

Reading Hamlet this week:

There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio,
Than are dreamt of in your philosophy.

Personally, I find the mysteriousness of the Universe provides life with intrigue.  It's vastness makes it feel unreal in a way, which gives us all hope that maybe someone's just playing a joke on us, because it can't be real.  I think the quantum guys suggest that may be the case.

comments.name: AFather
comments.body: Each time we launch another telescope into space: Hubble, James Webb and now the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, we learn more surprises. While this article includes conjectures, in a few months we may have a factual basis and thus know more about other possibly habitable worlds. The further we look, the more we see.

comments.name: AD
comments.body: We're like microbes on a grain of sand speculating about microbes on other grains far from us, unable to fathom the scale of the beach or the waves, or the sky rolling over us.

comments.name: Joel Fritz
comments.body: One of the sad things is that, assuming that the speed of light is a real cosmic speed limit, we may never get first hand evidence of the presence of intelligent life forms eksewher in the universe.  Given the magnitude of the universe it's not unreasonable to assume that intelligent life developed in at least one other place. We just may never encounter it. I've been reading science fiction since 1953 so the existence of other intelligent species is an element in the background of my consciousness.  I'm willing to suspend disbelief enough that I can enjoy stories with generation ships and FTL travel.  BTW, I say bring on the exoplanet stories.  I'm waiting for the 1 G CHON planets to show up.

comments.name: rosser

During my reporting, I came across many young voters who were eager to learn about new candidates from both parties. Many are familiar with Bobby Pulido's music and his now campaign for congress (He's a well known Tejano singer). comments.name: Dennis

comments.name: Clare Cy
comments.body: I think the big picture (or universal, catholic) approach to issues like abortion could alleviate some of the hostility in our politics.  I wonder how many “pro-life” people know that abortion rates decline when Democrats are president?  (Democrats typically have better economies and better social safety nets, including reproductive healthcare, than Republicans do.). Couldn’t the anti-legal abortion side and pro-choice side agree that making birth control readily available makes the rates of unintended pregnancy lower, which, in turn, lowers abortion rates?  Couldn’t they agree that a decent social safety net makes abortions for economic reasons less likely?  The beauty of this approach is that it actually works, unlike making abortion illegal, which tends to increase abortion rates.

comments.name: Paul

comments.name: Robert Bott
comments.body:
One of my favorite tours in North America -- from Astoria to San Luis Obispo in 2008 -- included this section, and I agree with the authors about its beauty and charm. That whole coast is great for cycling, and the many state parks are perfect for overnight stays in reserved hiker-biker areas where you can meet fellow travelers and share tales (and often meals and libations). 

Note: It is imperative to ride the West Coast from north to south, which puts you on the ocean side of the highway with the great views and pull-off areas. The prevailing winds are also from the northwest, and they usually strengthen in the afternoon to provide a welcome boost just as your energy flags. Perhaps the unhappiest riders I encountered were the group of German women who had chosen to ride from south to north.

Based on my years of touring that included 36 US states and all 10 Canadian provinces, I'd say that the only comparable cycling experience in North America would be the "Green Routes" in Quebec. Some other bucket-list possibilities would include the Allegheny and C&O Canal route from Pittsburgh to Washington DC, the Katy Trail in Missouri, and the trail network in Prince Edward Island.

Having the friend insist that she was reasonable and LW was not is dismissive, and would only heighten the emotional distress. 
LW, remember that relationships are a two way street. I hope you can chase the people who chase you.

comments.name: Someone
comments.body:
For LW1, the guest list is managed by the bride and groom and they chose guests they view as their intimate circle. The takeaway isn't that your friend doesn't consider you family. The son does not view you that way. Blaming your friend for that perception is unkind as she is not responsible for how her son and soon-to-be daughter in law view your role in their life. 

Lastly, you've been through a lot that you should absolutely discuss with a therapist and come up with a path forward to build your chosen family. That is something only you can do and isn't the responsibility of anyone else.

comments.name: Sam

Inflation is caused by many factors, but the main one right now is Trump's needless war in Iran driving up fuel prices, which in turn drives up many other prices.  It's hard to see how the Fed raising rates will solve this problem.  If they continue to raise rates, they're more likely to cause a recession than to drive down inflation, because the inflation is driven primarily by the war's fuel crisis, not by a "hot" economy.

comments.body:
This is the problem of a K shaped recovery, which Trump’s people at the Fed (and Treasury?) are denying. 

The money at the top being spent drives the numbers, but the people are at the bottom. Policies that look only at the spending figures only work with a flat or linear income distribution. We don’t have that.

By cutting social safety net spending, Trump made managing the economy more difficult. By his massive deficit spending to finance current consumption — and not infrastructure build-out, which is what Biden was doing — Trump has created a pernicious, broad-based, inflation problem that will be impossible to solve without a recession. 

Hate to say it, but only another Paul Volker can stop inflation now.

comments.name: Joseph Carmine Magnotti
comments.body: The invasion of Iraq by the United States under George W. Bush was probably the greatest military blunder in our history. The resources wasted in Iraq should have been concentrated in Afghanistan to bring the Taliban to a permanent end and to install a friendly government. Additionally, the attack on Iraq removed the main rival of Iran, which had fought a costly war with Iraq for eight years in the 1980s that ended in a stalemate. The invasion of Iraq is probably the single most important reason why Iran has become a dominant power in the region and the greatest state sponsor of terrorism in the world, not to mention the current war against the United States which has no end in sight.

comments.name: Otis
comments.body:
The Iranian regime might claim victory in this latest war but it will likely be a pyrrhic victory. 

The regime has spent billions of dollars supporting Hamas and Hezbollah only to have these two militias be decimated by Israel. Tomorrow, in fact, is the two year anniversary of the humiliating and devastating Israeli pager attack on Hezbollah. 

It has propped up the Houthis but the Houthis have turned into a kind of Frankenstein monster it can no longer control. It’s a matter of time before Saudi Arabia and Egypt (both of whom are suffering economically because of the Houthis) world decide to confront them head on. 

Iran lost a major ally and bridge to the Arab world when the Assad regime in Syria collapsed. 

Iran itself has suffered severe infrastructure and economic damage. The fact Israeli intelligence has such deep penetration of Iran shows how fragile it is. 

Once the bombs stop falling the Iranian regime - already by all accounts deeply unpopular - will have a lot of explaining to do to their own people about why so much of their money was wasted and why their economy is a shambles.

comments.name: AJS
comments.body:
The article 100% right. The overthrow of Saddam Hussein fundamentally altered the Middle Eastern balance of power. Iraq and Iran had fought a devastating eight-year war, and for decades Iraq had been an important counterweight to Iranian power in the Gulf. 
Then Bush came along...by removing Saddam and dismantling the Iraqi state without establishing an equally powerful stabilizing structure, he effectively eliminated Iran's principal regional military rival and created a political vacuum in which Tehran could expand its influence. 
The irony is striking: an intervention intended in part to make the Middle East more secure and to transform the region instead greatly strengthened one of America's principal regional adversaries. 
Ultimately, the roots of much of today's Middle Eastern turmoil lie in the Bush administration's deeply flawed policies, not least the decision to eliminate Saddam Hussein, a decision in which personal hostility toward Saddam appears to have played a significant role.

Linker's Substack is titled Notes from the Middleground and oh he tries so hard to be the sober middlegound pundit in assessing Klein and Taylor's text. Sadly for all of us his 'what if we took a more sober historical approach' is way off the mark for at least three reasons.
1. The fascist project in the US, rising yet again in historical terms, may well take control this time as Taylor and Klein and a varied host of others right and left warn. That precipice is here. Now.
2. Owners and leaders of AI empires *themselves* waver between fear for and confidence in a future that includes human beings (and presumably viable ecosystems which sustain us), some openly panicking *this week* over slowing AI development. Right now.
3. Climate cooking is well underway and accelerating, laws created to slow it being discarded. Corals, globally, have a decade left at best. Experts in atmospheric sciences try not to scare us all but they should. We are in a climate crisis never before seen nor having to be confronted. Globally.
Linker reminds me of an oil executive, a life-long friend, who over lunch agreed with all the concerns, saying "We will have to stop all of that, starting in 50-75 years." 
In the present moment sober means facing reality and dealing with it. Lions have entered the cave.
