comments.body:
History supports this. The interwar establishments that contained fascist movements did not out-charisma them. They absorbed the grievance through ordinary channels while refusing the movement's extra-legal instrument; kept the police and courts in their own hands; withdrew sanction from inside the movement's own base; united across party on the office, not a program; refused the cabinet seat with a referee attached; and reincorporated the flank the movement fed on. Weimar failed on the referee, not on rhetoric.

The test is symmetric: no rule passes unless you would accept it applied to you by your rival. Give your loyalty to the rules that let you contest power, not to the person who promises to wield it for you.

And if you are a new arrival in France, for exmple, without a bank account, you have to receive a French Carte de Sejour (CdS, Residency card) in order to open a bank account.  You cannot rent an apartment or get medical care or change your drivers license, or sign up for internet service or electricity  without a bank account and a CdS and a utility bill.  You are stuck paying for an AirBnB, which does not require either a CdS or a bank account, but charges accordingly.

You can, of course, sign up to pay income taxes and social charges without these documents.

But it takes at least 5 months to get a CdS, if you are already an EU citizen who supposed ly has the RIGHT to live in France, and who supposedly has the RIGHT, under EU law to receive one "immediately" (that is the word used by the EU regulation) upon request.  That happens only if they have no suspicions about your "papers", which are certified by other EU countries, but which France considers to be "suspicious" from the start. Your spouse and children can end up waiting for a year or more..

When you complain about the delays, you are advised to go use Revolut or one of the other online banks, because they don't have any qualms about giving you an account without the papers.  They also evidently, do not know the identities of the important people in various countries who might ask them for financial information about you.  One wonders who else they might be providing this information to.

The EU has become a total mess..

comments.name: A Doctor
comments.body:
In the original presentation of the statistical evidence, experts asserted that the chances of the data against Letby occurring by chance alone was infinitesimally small. After re-analysis by skeptical statisticians, the estimate dropped to a one in ten chance that the data was by chance alone. Not exactly an exoneration. And multiple other lines of evidence were also considered.

With respect to the assertion that exculpatory evidence was excluded in pre trial motions, this seems highly unlikely, as the judicial system usually rules in favor of the defendant. In addition, Letby testified extensively in defense of herself, and her council had opportunity to cross examine expert witnessed and provide their own. This did not apparently raise enough reasonable doubt in the minds of two juries. 

It seems unlikely that her conviction will be overturned.

comments.name: dr. paul

As such, I agree that having a "universal" (standard) language would also be efficiently beneficial, as it facilitates cross-border conversations and discussions in a way that simple translation cannot overcome (e.g., word nuance, use of double entendres).  But yet there has been little enthusiasm for such a language standard; how many speak or use Esperanto?  The reason, I would assert, is that language reflects one's national or regional (or even local) culture and distinctiveness, and we don't want to sacifice that for efficiency.  Language defines us and creates a bond with those who are "like us."  (And, I might add, while it also creates a barrier to those "others" who aren't like us, it reinforces a presumption of genetic Darwinian survival instincts....)

comments.name: 02ofL2
comments.body: Fungus gnats: even better than unsightly yellow sticky traps is to pick up a few pinguicula (butterwort) carnivorous plants. They are cute, throw up sweet-looking pink or purple flowers and absolutely entice fungus gnats like crazy. Many plant stores have them. Drosera (sundews) also work very well and have lovely white flowers when they bloom. I've found that small wide saracenias (pitcher plant) are a mealy bug magnate. Between the three of them, I've not had to police my 80+ orchids which I grow in the house. I'd not advise Venus fly traps, however, as fungus gnats are too quick for them to trigger the closing mechanism.

Fruit flies are having a Moment-- The October issue of The Atlantic has a poem by Jane Hirshfield responding to a fruit fly study of the flies' response (they lose weight and die) when surrounded by a great many of their conspecific dead: 

Abstract

Fruit flies exposed
to many dead fruit flies
lose their fat stores,
die more quickly
than those kept naive.
I who have lived long now
and will die of my living,
not of my grief,
and more than once
from a public garden
stole roses—
red ones and pink ones,
scented and not—
stammer before these
troubled and truthful fruit flies.

                   Jane Hirshfield

comments.name: Mary T
comments.body: The devices were pushed before the research was in ($$). Now we have the research (see The Digital Delusion for a review). The devices do not improve instruction and in many ways erode thinking and reading. Fine motor skills, closely linked to academic success are very poor. They are expensive and isolating. I’ve watched rooms full of students staring at screens (sometimes literally in the dark) rather than talking and thinking together. I’ve seen teachers spend repeated time explaining to children how to turn assignments in digitally when “pass your papers in” takes seconds. I had an analog childhood and the skills learned via face-to-face made it possible to adapt to whatever tech came along. Most of the time the tech is not used as a tool to augment problem solving—where the promise lies—but as sparkly worksheets. Currently 59 years in the ed business, K-12 to higher ed— and distressed to see what our children are being sold as quality education.

comments.name: Mac
comments.body:
In the early 1980s I read a book by the late Konstantin M. Simis, USSR: the Corrupt Society, the secret world of Soviet Capitalism. It was a detailed insider exposé detailing systemic bribery, the black market, and endemic graft across all levels of the Soviet political, legal, and economic systems. Simis had to flee the Soviet Union before this book was published, he had been a lawyer and judge.

Although published more than half a century ago, this book is still worth reading if you want to understand both former eastern block countries, and  Soviet Republics like Ukraine, Georgia, and of course, Russia itself. It’s important to understand how deeply corruption was inculcated into the political and administrative culture, and the  culture of the Soviet Union and of communist countries in eastern Europe (and China). There simply was a mindset that you were entitled to take your piece of the action - and at all business involved payoffs to somebody, and all administrators were entitled to line their pockets.

The reality is that this corruption remains deeply embedded in the political and business culture of the former Soviet states, and indeed the former eastern block. It’s so pervasive that people almost don’t notice it, it’s just presumed that payoffs and backhanders part of how the system works. That’s why rooting it out has proved so difficult even for Ukraine in a war and why so many have succumbed to corruption

comments.name: Pablo V
comments.body:
I'm in Kyrgyzstan right now. There is quite a bit of development happening, but on a relatively low level. Mentioned is that this 'skyscraper' is the first in the country's history (in fact, it's not the first one in Bishkek!). And it's not even a skyscraper in any substantive sense. By world standards, Kyrgyzstan is relatively poor economically, and you sense that when you're anywhere outside downtown Bishkek. 

By way of contrast, I was recently in Almaty, Kazakhstan. You truly feel like you're in a modern city. 'Skyscrapers' (tall apartment buildings) everywhere. Of course, Kazakhstan is a much larger and richer country; 5x greater GDP PPP. A key point of contrast: Kazakhstan does a lot of trade with the EU and a lot of its foreign debt is held by countries other than China and Russia. A lot of its oil goes to the EU.

Much of Kyrgyzstan's future will depend on its relationship to China. The latter holds a significant chunk of Kyrgyzstan's foreign debt, and is its largest trading partner. Much of the Kyrgyz economy depends on the movement of Chinese goods onwards to Russia. 

As with so many countries, young people flock to the cities in the good times to get a piece of the action, and more rural areas suffer. So when the war ends (if it ends), where do you go when jobs are scarce again? On to Russia to start from the bottom again? The war is a temporary economic prop.

comments.name: Mike Mc Cowan
comments.body:
AI can replace a lot of entry-level legwork. But after years in finance, I’ve learned there’s a huge difference between processing information and exercising judgment.   

Let AI gather the data, crunch the numbers, flag the risks and prepare the analysis.   

Then put a human being’s name on the final decision.  

AI makes a great assistant. It makes a lousy person to hold accountable when the decision blows up.

Hello American Express....

comments.body: I agree that education is an important step in life, but the real test is how one handles their job/work and  grows by taking on increasingly difficult tasks.    Often failing before finally succeeding.   Ones value to the organization is what they are capable of doing.  That comes from experience.

comments.name: James Thorleifson
comments.body:
“The training ground of entry-level work will shift under AI, but it won’t disappear… The most valuable employees won’t necessarily be the ones who can do their jobs without AI. They will be the ones who know how to use it and when.”

Bingo. Go to the head of the class, Mr. Broeder. 😃

I’m mostly retired these days, but I still do a bit of high level consulting. More as an avocation than a vocation, honestly. But it keeps me from going stir crazy. I’m currently doing some part time pipeline and utility GIS consulting for one our nation’s largest technical consulting firms.

This summer I volunteered to take one of this firm’s interns under my wing. This company has a major initiative underway to incorporate AI into all of their work. Accordingly, I encouraged my young padawan learner to incorporate AI into the completion of all her tasks.

She passed with flying colors. To the point of getting the corporate AI instance to function as an ad hoc knowledge graph database, producing typical knowledge graph display outputs on the complex datasets she was tasked with unraveling. This young lady now has a job waiting for her when she graduates.

The takeaway is simple, young college student. If you want a job, learn to use AI to do something more productive than cheat on tests and homework assignments. Learn to use and collaborate with AI to further and enhance the outcomes of real work. Do that, and write your own ticket. 😃

comments.name: James Russell
comments.body: All of these essays are variations of the same theme.  People skills and classical education are the way forward to beat AI.  I disagree. Executives and managers "didn’t rise because they were really good at spreadsheets." Actually, they did. Spreadsheets were the AI of the late 1980s/early 90s. An accountant, actuary or engineer who decided to forsake spreadsheets and focus on his calculator and "people skills" would not see very many promotions.  Students today should not be doubling down on classical education to deal with AI in the workforce.  They should be doubling down on STEM classes and building technical expertise.  All the while using AI to help them get there.

comments.name: Matt Olson
comments.body:
The people of many countries consider themselves unique. Of course, usually in a positive way. Most of the time this attitude is exaggerated, even if understandable.
But it is more true for Japan far more than most. Diversity can be a plus, but not always. Immigration can be a plus, but it can also be disastrous, as it has been for Sweden.
Some consider national pride in specific cultural attitudes and habits anachronistic and arrogant, but it's valid for the citizens of a country to decide their own destiny, however unwoke that may be.
Imagine how well most American immigrants would conform to Japanese values. Not very well, I think. I taught English there. Now consider, let's say, Syrians and Pakistanis. It would be catastrophic.
It's better for Japan, as the vast majority of its people want, to  retain it homogeneous identity. Fewer working age demographics  may mean some economic hardship, but for Japan, it's probably worth it.

Which a current trend in Japan is turning against. How foolish to turn against immigration, then--as in the US--when it could bolster an economy becoming difficult due to taking care of the elderly? comments.name: Riley Temple
comments.body: I have experienced August Wilson's plays for many years of my adult life, and I have published essays about his plays. Over the years two actors emerge as skilled and inspired Wilson interpreters.  First there is Stephen McKinley Henderson and then Reuben Santiago-Hudson. Both seem to have mastered the peerless Wilson soliloquy cadence and each elevates a Wilson speech to rhapsody.  I recently saw the New York production of "Joe Turner's Come and Gone."  Santiago-Hudson played Bynum.  Not long after the first act begins, Bynum delivers a speech about his dream of the Shiny Man.  It is here that Wilson establishes the centrality of finding one's song - one's identity -- to be truly free. Santiago-Hudson's Bynum spoke to highlight Wilson's abundant lyrical gifts. The speech was inspired and sublime. No actor has performed it with such understanding of and love for August Wilson. I wept in honor of that transcendence.

Secret Chinese permanent underwater cables and submersibles have been found off our northern shores that are designed to warn China if any of our (few) subs tried to go to the aid of Taiwan if the CCP invaded.  China has engaged in direct economic coercion against Australian industries.  The CCP have been building Navy-suitable deep sea ports in Pacific nations, and stationing their police their, in countries that are not far from our North-Eastern shores, even though they are very far from China. The bottom line is that China could so easily ring-fence Australia in a naval blockade and starve us of everything that we need to import currently like fuel, food, fertiliser, technology, etc.  Australia took our long-term historical friendly Pacific neighbour relationships for granted and has desperately been playing catch up to try and maintain our sovereignty and avoid falling totally under China's indirect (or direct) control.

comments.name: Michael
comments.body:
I just finished planning an extensive five week independent trip to China (first time there) and used AI to plan my itinerary (note: I'd hardly used AI for research before this).

The results: very detailed and impressive first draft!  Saved me weeks of initial planning "the old fashioned way."  

I did much of what this article recommended.  Primary tip:  it is important to vet and refine your AI results.  Involve real human input!  My spouse and I talked with others who visited China, read online travel discussions and guides, and even found a travel consultant (in China) to review our AI results.  We continue to work on our AI-generated plan for correctness, timeliness, and details.

Can't wait to start the trip and test it out!

comments.name: UWS couple
comments.body: We used Claude for a recent trip.  It was very good over all.  In particular, the tool took in and organized all the various reservation information I fed it in pdf, email and screenshot format and presented it in a nice, logical fashion.  Additionally, Claude kept a running list of open actions and even highlighted a few items that we did not notice, such as a double booked itinerary and missing hotel night.  Agree with Seth though...  it took some trial and error to get the tool thinking about restaurants we preferred and sights we enjoyed and worked much better as we gave it more detailed information.  Directing the tool to ask you clarifying questions helped a lot too.  What tips have you discovered?

comments.body: Sleep rituals are pretty demanding if you need to stick by the same thing everyday, though I never understood the need for an exact routine that a person should follow or else they can't sleep, the only real "routine" that I follow it showering and brushing my teeth before bed. I have heard that some people need a certain type of sound needs to play when falling asleep, but for me I just like down and stay there until I fall asleep and wake up the next day. I do admire the fact that some people follow a routine everyday, but I never really followed a routine and a small change in anything didn't really affect me where I can't fall asleep.

comments.name: Jacob Dorador
comments.body: I don't really have sleep rituals, it is more like a schedule I shower then time on my phone then sleep, none of it is really meant to prepare me for bed, rather just get a dopamine spike before the lights shut off. I'm not happy with them, however time I have after school is limited and I am not someone who plans ahead. Falling asleep is something I struggle with often, I find myself tossing in bed, waking up stressed and exhausted when I should feel refreshed. I'm open to the rituals or habits others have shared, but I really don't think they would do much to help me fall asleep, as for advice to others struggling with falling asleep, I don't think I'm in a place to give advice.

comments.name: Isla Polakoff
comments.body: This article asks about everyone’s specific night time sleep rituals, I believe everyone has their own but mine is very specific, it is so much a part of my life that i actually have a difficult time falling asleep when i don’t follow it step by step in the correct order every night. My sleep ritual brings me both comfort and stress, it brings comfort to the idea of having a routine, because I like routines, but also stress to the idea that if it's not done I'm likely not falling asleep. Every night when my 9:30 pm alarm goes off I know it's time for me to get ready for bed, I use the same makeup remover, then the same face wash, then brush my teeth. After that i hop in the shower, and then put on lotion, and a special sleep face mask, and then i cant fall asleep without an ice cold glass of water next to my bed, i wont end up drinking it but i like the comfort of having it in case I want it.

comments.name: Mason

After I finish all of that, I’m usually pretty tired, either because of the fact that I’m tired of doing work, or simply because I have my gym class the last period of the day. Due to this, I normally both shower, and brush my teeth before bed because I like feeling clean. Even after all of that, I still only get 4 hours of sleep and feel exhausted in the morning.

comments.name: Joel M.
comments.body:
Sleeping to me has come to be quite difficult as I would want to keep scrolling or playing games but eventually we will have to sleep. So things I do to sleep, or as you call sleep rituals, is first a 10-30 minute walk around my apartments(multiple apartments are connected, making it spacious, and are gated, making it quite safe) and lastly, a little scroll on my phone (its irresistible).

My sleep rituals for the most part are good and cheer me up as I always see something peculiar on these walks whether its something cool in someones balcony or a stranger I chat with who follow my path for a bit before parting. These sleep rituals of mine never existed up until I moved to my new apartments but the day I  established these routines for myself, it has helped me sleep as sleep for me is very difficult. 

Most of the times, before these rituals. I used to get like 3 to 5 hours of sleep, making the work I do very poor as a result of poor sleep. In these times, it affected me mentally as I just couldn't keep up with the loads of work with little as 3 hours of sleep (it was impossible). My sleep ritual is pretty great and if I were to add something new, it would probably be something like origami because, for me, the haste of which some origami people make it is insane and learning that will be so awesome.

As a teenager myself, I would like to say to other teenagers that sleep is very important and setting these sleep rituals will help you get your much needed rest for school.

comments.name: Rihanna G.
comments.body: I wish my sleep schedule was better. Schoolwork and studying take up a lot of my night, so I usually only get around five hours of sleep. Sometimes I’m so exhausted that I fall asleep while doing my homework. My sleep problems are both caused by my busy schedule and made worse by my difficulty falling asleep once I finally get to bed because that’s where I can gain free-time. While I know staying up at night getting my assignments finished is important, it also makes it harder to focus, lowers my energy, and makes me more stressed during the day. If I could give advice to other teenagers it would be that school matters, and sleep matters too. It is easy to focus on one and ignore the other but both are necessary.

comments.name: Rudy Hartung
comments.body:
The article’s central correction is right: speculative extinction scenarios must not distract from the harms being created by AI systems now. But there is a further, more practical point.
Today’s advanced AI is like an excellent pilot in an excellent aircraft—without a checklist. It can be fluent, fast and apparently knowledgeable, yet it cannot reliably distinguish a verified fact from a plausible invention, nor can it independently prove that its data are complete, current or relevant. Asking the model to “check itself” does not solve this; it is the student grading its own exam.
That is why the priority should be neither apocalypse rhetoric nor blind deregulation, but verifiable middleware: external gates for data provenance, freshness, completeness, deterministic cross-checks and human accountability. In critical applications, the system must be allowed to say: “I cannot establish this reliably; do not act on my output.”
I work on critical AI for tactical firefighting. There, a hallucinated hydrant location, stale wind data or an unsupported fire-spread forecast is not an abstract alignment problem—it can place responders in danger. The EU AI Act is defensible precisely when understood this way: not as a brake on intelligence, but as a requirement for the checklist, audit trail and independent verification layer that a responsible engineer should demand before deploying AI where lives depend on it.

"It remains to be seen just how effective the new beach will be in protecting the coast in the long run,"

I think we already know how effective it will be. The NASA glaciologist Eric Rignot has stated that we’ve already destabilized around 20 feet of sea level rise equivalent of ice from the marine sectors of Greenland and West Antarctica’s ice sheets and the much larger East Antarctic Ice Sheet is waking up and it has 62 feet worth of marine based ice.

One problem with sea level rise is the closer sea levels approach the top of a coastal defense the greater the risk of a storm surge breaching the defense and the damage occurs as in New Orleans with Hurricane Kartrina. As a result many of our large coastal cities won’t go slowly with sea level rise, but quickly in catastrophic storms.

From a few years ago: “Today, we’re struggling with 3 millimeters [0.1 inch] per year [of sea level rise],” says Robert DeConto at the University of Massachusetts-Amherst, co-author of one of the more sobering new studies. “We’re talking about centimeters per year. That’s really tough. At that point your engineering can’t keep up; you’re down to demolition and rebuilding.”

It’s time we started planning a managed retreat from vulnerable coastal areas rather than wasting billions on coastal defenses under the mistaken impression that we can hold back the ocean.

https://e360.yale.edu/features/abrupt_sea_level_rise_realistic_greenland_antarctica

comments.body: Great article. My grandfather was from Lulea and I  spent several days above the Arctic Circle in Sweden last summer. The beauty of the landscape is sublime. The people are friendly and relaxed in their skin in the ways that maybe we were once. I reminisce about the many trails like this one that we've lost all over the world in the last hundred years. Thank god some still remain.

comments.name: Tmn
comments.body:
Thank you for this article and the photos. I recognize the descriptions and some of the huts! I had the pleasure and good fortune to be in Luleå for work a few years back with some vacation time tacked on the back end... on a whim I solo hiked the Kings Trail. 

It was summer solstice with its 24 hrs of daylight above the arctic circle, which is considered pre-season so all the huts had an available bed for me each night (no advanced reservations needed). I took as long as I wanted each day to get to the next hut, or sit out a rain storm in one of the warming huts, sit and watch the reindeer herds, or take detours to climb up various nearby peaks.  It truly a treasure of the trail. Especially of note is the crossing of rather large lakes necessary further on the trail, either by Sami driven motor boat or (if you're in the mood cause you have the time) by the provided row boats. 

I have told everyone I hike with to try and plan a trip to the Kings Trail; it and the people you meet are that wonderful!

comments.name: Jenn
comments.body:
The "rogue AI" is not representative of all of machine learning and is not nearly as inevitable as the LLM companies want to pretend. In fact, every instance of a "rogue AI" I've heard of so far involves negligence on the part of the AI company: they are leaving these programs in loops with powerful tools, impossible or nearly impossible tasks, and no human supervision for extended periods of time. As Cal Newport has said, they're tieing a weed-whacker to a dog and then acting surprised when chaos results. That they then pretend that the chaos is inevitable is just insulting.

The only difficulty these companies have reining in their "rogue AI" is that acknowledging that they're not developing a superintelligent digital deity will hurt their stock prices.

comments.body: Re kosher "Lamb testicles squish like sweetbreads, but taste of iron and embers. " - are very hard to find because most male lambs raised for commercial meat are castrated when they are very young. Under Jewish law, removing a limb or organ from a living animal is strictly forbidden (ever min hachai), meaning testicles harvested from routine live-castration methods are not kosher.
